stories.title: Inflation Fell. So Why Is Your Bill Still High?

beats.narration: Inflation fell. So why does your grocery bill still feel high?
beats.asset: real supermarket receipt or checkout; license review required

beats.narration: Because the inflation rate and the price level are not the same.
beats.asset: real moving grocery price shelf; license review required

beats.narration: The inflation rate hit 9.1 percent in June 2022.
beats.asset: K70 original press card over licensed moving footage

beats.narration: The rate later slowed. But the price index did not return to its old level.
beats.asset: BLS CPI-U line chart, separate rate versus price-level labels

beats.narration: Slower price increases don't erase the increases you already paid.
Watch the cumulative price level, not only the inflation headline.
beats.asset: BLS CPI-U price index with correctly sourced base period

beats.narration: Rent, fuel, and groceries follow different price paths.
beats.asset: rent sign or gas pump, rights cleared

beats.narration: The pace changed. The price level didn't reset.
Which expense changed the most for you?
beats.asset: large readable question over last licensed footage shot

news.headline: Developing economies paid $415B in external debt interest in 2024

beats.narration: Four hundred fifteen billion dollars. Just in interest.
That's what low- and middle-income countries paid on external debt in 2024.
The World Bank reported that staggering interest bill.
beats.asset: original K70 newspaper-style card over footage

beats.narration: The reported bill rose from about 406 billion in 2023.
beats.asset: source-backed 2023 vs 2024 interest payment comparison; match coverage

beats.narration: Interest absorbs funding that governments could use elsewhere.
And it pays for the cost of debt—not a new hospital or school.
beats.asset: big $415B counter; label it 2024 external debt interest

beats.narration: Borrowing costs make a huge difference.
The shock isn't only what countries owe. It's the price of carrying it.
Which matters more: less debt or lower borrowing costs?
